name: Quapaw
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Rankin, Robert L. 2005. 'Quapaw', in Hardy & Scancarelli (eds.), Native Languages of the Southeastern United States (Univ. of Nebraska Press) — sketch by the principal Quapaw documenter; not online. Wikipedia Quapaw phonology (read) has no stress statement.

new_statements.quote: 5.5. Accent. Accent is distinctive in Quapaw. Most investigators have analyzed Mississippi Valley Siouan accentual systems as simple stress (amplitude) systems. [...] In general, Quapaw preserves the second syllable (iambic) accent rule, but because of the syncope of initial syllable vowels in certain forms throughout Mississippi Valley Siouan, there are numerous exceptions to the rule. Generally one can expect to find initial syllable accent in stative verb stems, body part terms, and in words beginning with a tense stop or any consonant cluster, as such forms quite generally had an initial syllable vowel that has been lost. Accent in verbs is especially fluid, often moving leftward as prefixes are added.
new_statements.citation: Rankin, Robert L. 2005. Quapaw. In Heather K. Hardy & Janine Scancarelli (eds.), Native Languages of the Southeastern United States, 454-498. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default accent on the second syllable from the left (inherited MVS iambic rule), written by Rankin as stress; accent is nonetheless described as distinctive because historical syncope of initial-syllable vowels yields many initial-accented words (stative verb stems, body-part terms, words beginning with a tense/geminate stop or a consonant cluster); in verbs accent shifts leftward as prefixes are added. Rankin notes a pitch-accent analysis (as for Proto-Siouan and possibly Omaha) 'may be possible for Quapaw'.
new_statements.exceptions: Numerous exceptions with initial-syllable accent: stative verb stems, body-part terms, words beginning with a tense stop or any consonant cluster (forms that lost an initial-syllable vowel by syncope); accent in verbs 'especially fluid', moving leftward with prefixation; Dorsey's accent markings 'a bit strange in a number of cases'. Sec. 5.4: distinctive vowel length with both accented and unaccented long vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent; compound deictics 'are accented as single words' (p. ~474). Author flags that 'accent is distinctive' and that the system may be pitch accent rather than stress; catalogers may prefer 'lexical with second-syllable default' over strictly fixed-second. Data from last fluent speakers (1973-74) plus Dorsey's 1880s-90s BAE materials.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Quapaw proper (quap1242; autonym Okáxpa), Dhegiha Siouan, based on Rankin's 1973-74 fieldwork with the last fluent speakers near Miami, Oklahoma plus J. O. Dorsey's 1880s-90s BAE materials; no dialect split. Language now dormant.

sources.note: Sec. 5.5 'Accent' (pp. 465-466): accent is distinctive; MVS systems usually analyzed as stress but Proto-Siouan likely pitch accent on 2nd syllable, and a pitch-accent analysis 'may be possible for Quapaw'; written as simple stress; Quapaw generally preserves the second-syllable (iambic) accent rule, with numerous exceptions from initial-vowel syncope (initial accent in stative verb stems, body-part terms, words beginning with tense stop or cluster); accent in verbs fluid, moving leftward as prefixes are added. Sec. 5.4: distinctive vowel length, both accented and unaccented long vowels.
